raw_case_text:
An 8-year-old girl, from a rural area in Choco (Colombian Pacific Coast), presented with 20 days of fever, hiporexia, asthenia, and arthralgias, associated with emesis and diarrhea. She was found to have anemia and was prescribed ferrous bisglycinate without improvement. The fever was persistent and was associated with chills, abdominal pain, and dark urine; she was admitted to a rural hospital and diagnosed with pancytopenia; 2 units of packed red blood cells were transfused; and she was transferred to our hospital with a clinical suspicion of lymphoproliferative disorder. Her vital signs showed tachycardia (131 bpm), tachypnea (45 per min), and limit-low oxygen saturation (91%). Physical examination revealed jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly of 6 cm and of 2 cm below the costal margin, respectively; fine right basal crackles and a soft systolic heart murmur were heard at the left sternal border and the third intercostal space. Her past medical history was relevant for posttraumatic osteomyelitis of the right humerus and septic arthritis of the right elbow; her parents were not consanguineous, and she did not have pseudoalbinism.
Test results revealed thrombocytopenia and lymphopenia (Hg 11.5 g/dL, WBCs 4600/microL, neutrophils 3404/microL, lymphocytes 1058/microL, and platelets 59000/microL), elevated C-reactive protein (21.57 mg/dL), and altered liver function tests (ALT 349 U/L, AST 135 U/L, total bilirubin 6.67 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.3 mg/dL, LDH 1376 IU/L, and albumin 2.1 g/dL). Infectious workup was negative for HIV, dengue, malaria, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, CMV, EBV, and Mycoplasma. Additional laboratory tests showed hypertriglyceridemia (787 mg/dL) and hyperferritinemia (>2000 ng/mL) with normal fibrinogen (311 mg/dL). Echocardiogram showed minimal pericardial effusion and preserved ventricular function without anatomic defects or signs of endocarditis. Abdominal ultrasound showed a small right pleural effusion, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and retroperitoneal and hepatic hilar lymphadenopathies. Abdominal computed tomography showed the same findings, with hypodensity areas corresponding to splenic infarcts. She was diagnosed with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and started on piperacillin-tazobactam and intravenous immunoglobulin (1 g/kg/d for 2 days); while waiting for blood cultures and bone marrow analysis, CSF was within normal limits. On her third hospital night, she presented hematemesis and rectorrhagia with hypovolemic shock that required fluid resuscitation, intravenous infusion of omeprazole, tranexamic acid, phytomenadione, packed red blood cell, and platelets transfusion. She was stabilized; upper and lower endoscopies did not show signs of active bleeding, but just some residual melena. On the fourth day of hospitalization, both blood and bone marrow cultures were positive for Salmonella typhi; and the antibiotic regimen was changed to ciprofloxacin; bone marrow specimen showed hematopoietic precursors with no signs of malignancy; and no hemophagocytosis was appreciated. Repeated blood cultures were negative; during the hospital stay, she was started on enalapril to maintain a tight control on blood pressure. She completed 14 days of antibiotic treatment with resolution of the fever, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and the abdominal pain. Laboratory investigations before discharge showed resolution of the cytopenias, down trending of liver function tests and triglycerides levels, and ferritin was still elevated.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old girl from rural Chocó, Colombia, presented with a 20-day history of persistent fever, hyporexia, asthenia, arthralgias, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, chills, and dark urine.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed fever, hyporexia, asthenia, arthralgias, emesis, and diarrhea 20 days prior to admission. She was initially diagnosed with anemia and prescribed oral ferrous bisglycinate without improvement. As her fever persisted alongside chills, abdominal pain, and dark urine, she was admitted to a rural hospital where pancytopenia was noted; she received 2 units of packed red blood cells and was transferred to our institution for suspected lymphoproliferative disorder. On her third hospital night, she developed acute upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding (hematemesis and rectorrhagia) with hypovolemic shock.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of post-traumatic osteomyelitis of the right humerus and septic arthritis of the right elbow. From a rural area on the Colombian Pacific Coast (Chocó). Parents were non-consanguineous; no history of pseudoalbinism.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 20-day fever, chills, hyporexia, asthenia, arthralgias, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dark urine, jaundice, and subsequent hematemesis and rectorrhagia. Prior medication: ferrous bisglycinate.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, vital signs showed tachycardia (131 bpm), tachypnea (45 breaths/min), and borderline-low oxygen saturation (91%). Physical examination revealed jaundice, hepatomegaly (6 cm below the costal margin), splenomegaly (2 cm below the costal margin), fine right basal lung crackles, and a soft systolic murmur at the left sternal border (third intercostal space).
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL (post-transfusion), WBC 4,600/µL, neutrophils 3,404/µL, lymphopenia (lymphocytes 1,058/µL), and thrombocytopenia (platelets 59,000/µL). Inflammatory and HLH markers: CRP 21.57 mg/dL, hypertriglyceridemia 787 mg/dL, hyperferritinemia >2,000 ng/mL, and normal fibrinogen 311 mg/dL. LFTs showed ALT 349 U/L, AST 135 U/L, total bilirubin 6.67 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.3 mg/dL, LDH 1,376 IU/L, and hypoalbuminemia (albumin 2.1 g/dL). Infectious screens for HIV, dengue, malaria, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, CMV, EBV, and Mycoplasma were negative. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed minimal pericardial effusion and preserved ventricular function without vegetations. Abdominal ultrasound showed a small right pleural effusion, hepatosplenomegaly, and retroperitoneal and hepatic hilar lymphadenopathy.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT confirmed small right pleural effusion, hepatosplenomegaly, retroperitoneal and hepatic hilar lymphadenopathy, and wedge-shaped splenic hypodensities consistent with splenic infarcts. Lumbar puncture/CSF analysis was normal. Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopies (performed after stabilization of hospital day 3 GI hemorrhage) showed residual melena without active bleeding sites. Bone marrow aspiration/biopsy showed normal hematopoietic precursors without malignancy or hemophagocytosis. On hospital day 4, both blood and bone marrow cultures grew Salmonella typhi.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe typhoid fever complicated by secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)-like syndrome, splenic infarcts, hepatitis, and upper/lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage with hypovolemic shock, confirmed by positive blood and bone marrow cultures for Salmonella typhi. Hematologic malignancy, HIV, dengue, malaria, viral hepatitis, CMV, EBV, and Mycoplasma were ruled out. Initially managed empirically for suspected HLH/sepsis with piperacillin-tazobactam and IVIG (1 g/kg/day for 2 days) and resuscitated on night 3 for GI bleeding (IV fluids, omeprazole infusion, tranexamic acid, vitamin K/phytomenadione, and PRBC/platelet transfusions), her antibiotic regimen was switched on day 4 to targeted ciprofloxacin for 14 days (plus enalapril for blood pressure control). Repeat blood cultures cleared, fever, hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal pain, and cytopenias resolved, and liver enzymes and triglycerides trended down prior to discharge.
